FIRST MANUSCRIPT PACKAGE

One expression.
One complete composition.

An opening essay and two sample chapters, approximately 6,075 words including notes. The chapters separate textual observation, interpretation, evaluation, and the further question of origin.

Independent Arabic review, stronger comparative evidence, original reader studies, and the full manuscripts.

An invitation to examine

Opening essay · Draft 0.1 · 16 September 2026

You need not begin this book by believing that the Qur’an is divine. Begin with a passage. Attend to what it says, how it says it, and what changes when its expression changes. Then ask how much that observation supports.

That is a modest beginning for a large claim. The Qur’an does not merely invite admiration. It presents itself as revelation and issues a challenge to those who doubt it. In 2:23 the challenge concerns producing a comparable surah. In 17:88 the claim extends to the combined efforts of humans and jinn. These passages establish the claim we are investigating. They do not, simply by being quoted, settle its truth. Qur’an 2:23, 17:88

The argument therefore asks more of us than noticing that a text is unusual. Every substantial work differs from other works in some respects. An unusual expression can be clumsy; a familiar one can be excellent. Nor does excellence by itself tell us that its author is more than human. Human literature offers extraordinary achievements, and a serious argument for revelation must make room for that fact.

Four propositions must remain separate: this text is distinctive; this text achieves something exceptional; the achievement is beyond human productive capacity, including exceptional genius; and revelation explains its origin. Each requires its own reasons. Neither the third nor the fourth can be borrowed from the first two without further argument. A comparative study may inform the case while remaining unable to establish universal human incapacity on its own.

We will begin with a sentence in a prayer. An old man speaks of weakness in his bones and a head overtaken by gray hair. The language turns grayness into a blaze. A reader may notice the image immediately. A more careful reading asks what happens when the head itself becomes the grammatical subject of that blazing, and how the image belongs to the prayer around it. The first sample chapter examines that question through a classical account of arrangement and meaning.

Then we will move to a complete composition. Al-ʿAṣr contains an oath, a judgment of loss, and an exception that includes both personal action and mutual counsel. Its brevity makes its structure inspectable. It also makes it tempting to confuse a striking interpretation with an exhaustive one. We will resist that temptation by considering the range of readings offered by commentators and by distinguishing grammatical observation from a claim about its effect.

Readers who know Arabic will be able to inspect some of these judgments directly. Readers who do not will need more explanation. A transparent translation can expose part of the reasoning, but it cannot reproduce every relation of sound, grammar, and convention. The aim is neither to hide behind expertise nor to pretend expertise is unnecessary. We should identify which judgments can be checked from an explanation and which require independent linguistic review.

The book will sometimes ask you to compare a passage with a deliberately plain reformulation. Such an exercise is a lens. It helps isolate a particular choice. It is not an adequate contest between the Qur’an and the best that human authors can produce. A weak paraphrase loses because it is weak. The comparative investigation must therefore bring in accomplished human compositions and allow them to display their own strengths.

It must also allow the Qur’an to be recognizable. Readers familiar with it cannot simply forget what they are reading because an experiment removes the title. Familiarity, devotion, and literary competence can coexist, but they are different influences. Our studies will record recognition and background rather than promise a blindness they cannot deliver.

Numbers can help when the question is precise. We can count a specified kind of repetition. We can examine how a defined alteration changes readers’ comprehension. We can compare judgments across passages, readers, and reciters. But a number answers the question built into its definition. A count of repeated words is not a measure of wisdom. A classifier that recognizes Qur’anic style has learned to distinguish samples; it has not discovered revelation.

The first computational appendix is intentionally elementary. It documents the source text, its numbered units, and the rules used to count written tokens. Its purpose is to make the analysis reproducible and reveal assumptions that attractive numerical claims often conceal. It supplies no score of literary excellence.

The larger argument will depend on the relationships among several kinds of evidence. Literary analysis must demonstrate actual achievements. Comparative research must ask whether the achievements remain exceptional under fair conditions. Historical work must independently examine the circumstances relevant to composition and transmission. Philosophical reasoning must then explain why revelation accounts for the resulting evidence better than the strongest available alternatives.

An exceptional human author is one of those alternatives. So are accounts involving inherited forms, a religious and linguistic environment, oral performance, and processes of composition or transmission. Their adequacy must be evaluated rather than dismissed by definition. Revelation, in turn, must not function as an empty label for whatever a current model fails to explain. The case for it requires substantive reasons.

This is an affirmative investigation. It aims to articulate the strongest responsible case for revelation. That purpose does not require protecting every familiar argument. If a numerical claim depends on changing the counting rule after seeing the answer, it should lose its place. If a historical premise is weaker than commonly reported, the book should say so. If a literary interpretation survives serious alternatives, it should receive the weight it earns.

The reader’s task is not to admire on command. It is to follow the evidence far enough to judge what has been shown, what remains contestable, and what further inference is justified. Our first task is simpler still: to read one expression carefully.

The Head Ablaze

Sample chapter. Research draft dated 16 September 2026. Arabic and translations require independent specialist review before a reviewed edition. Translations without an attributed translator are original working renderings.

An old man is praying. Before he asks for what he needs, he describes what age has done to him. His strength is failing. His hair has whitened. Yet the sentence in which he speaks does something more particular than report those facts:

وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا

Wa-shtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban.

An image-preserving translation is: “And the head has blazed with gray hair.” The final word is pronounced shaybā when stopping on it. The Arabic is the middle clause of Qur’an 19:4. C19-01: Arabic passage

The expression is unfamiliar enough in English to invite a second look. A head does not ordinarily blaze with grayness. Why describe aging through fire? Why make the head, rather than the hair, the subject? And what does this image contribute to a prayer?

These questions can be investigated before deciding whether the Qur’an is revelation. We need not pretend that the theological question is unimportant. It is the larger question of this book. But a reader should be able to inspect the evidence offered in its support. Calling a sentence miraculous cannot replace explaining how it works.

This chapter therefore begins with a small, examinable claim: the relationship between the grammar and the image contributes to a recognizable literary effect. Whether that effect is admirable is a further judgment. Whether it belongs to a sustained achievement beyond human productive capacity is further still.

A sentence inside a prayer

The speaker is Zakariyyā, or Zechariah. Verses 19:2–3 introduce the account as a remembrance of divine mercy and describe his private calling upon his Lord. Verse 4 gives his words. In verses 5–6 he expresses concern about those who will follow him, describes his wife as unable to bear children, and asks for a successor who will inherit and be pleasing to God. The precise character of the inheritance is an exegetical question; nothing in the present argument requires settling it. C19-01: 19:2–6

Here is verse 4 in ordinary vocalized Arabic spelling, with the additional signs of the displayed muṣḥaf omitted:

قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا وَلَمْ أَكُنْ بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا

He said: “My Lord, my bones have weakened, and the head has blazed with gray hair. In calling upon You, my Lord, I have never been wretched.”

This working translation preserves the fire image while making one grammatical accommodation: Arabic has the singular al-ʿaẓm, “the bone,” where the translation uses “my bones.” Its final sentence deliberately stays close to the wording; the familiar sense of not having been disappointed in prayer is an interpretation supported by al-Ṭabarī’s commentary. C19-02: morphology, C19-04: commentary on 19:4

The verse can be read as moving from diminished bodily strength to visible aging and then to remembered confidence in God. That is the reading developed here, not a diagram supplied by the text. It has a basis readers can check: the order of the clauses, the physical descriptions, and the final statement about prayer. The apparent obstacle to Zakariyyā’s request and his reason for making it are brought together.

What the grammar lets us see

The central clause has three written words. That count uses the ordinary spacing of the Arabic, including the prefixed conjunction within the first word; it is not a claim about a uniquely correct linguistic tokenization.

Arabic element Basic function What the reader receives
وَاشْتَعَلَ “And blazed”: conjunction plus a past-tense verb A happening pictured through ignition or blazing
الرَّأْسُ “The head”: nominative noun, grammatical subject of the verb The head as the thing of which blazing is predicated
شَيْبًا “Grayness” or “gray hair”: accusative indefinite noun The respect in which the head has blazed

The case and verb information can be checked in the Quranic Arabic Corpus. The interpretation of the last word as a specifying accusative, tamyīz, follows the grammatical analysis developed in the classical discussion below. The Corpus’s word-by-word page identifies its accusative case; that fact alone is not a complete analysis of its syntactic function. C19-02

On the tamyīz analysis, grayness specifies an otherwise surprising attribution: the head has blazed, in respect of gray hair. It is not an object that the head burns. Nor is “head” an agent deliberately performing an action. “Grammatical subject” describes its role in the sentence, not a claim about intention or physical causation.

This distinction matters because loose explanations can turn an intelligible construction into a false mystery. Arabic is not violating its grammar here. It is using a grammatical possibility to present a relationship in a particular way.

Al-Ṭabarī also preserves a useful complication. He reports disagreement over the accusative shayban: one analysis takes it as a verbal noun expressing the sense of becoming gray; another treats it as specification or explanation. The existence of this disagreement does not remove the head’s grammatical role. It does prevent us from presenting one account of the final accusative as the only analysis ever available. C19-04

Al-Jurjānī’s invitation to compare

The attribution of this example to ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī can be made precise. In Dalāʾil al-iʿjāz, paragraphs 91–93 of Maḥmūd Muḥammad Shākir’s edition, he argues that naming the metaphor does not adequately explain the expression’s merit. The construction matters: the verb is attributed to the head, with grayness following in specification. He contrasts this with formulations making gray hair the subject and explains the Qur’anic construction through the idea of pervasive spread. He also discusses the definite expression “the head,” whose possessor is understood from context. The passage is on printed pages 100–102 of the third edition, 1413 AH / 1992. These pages and the edition statement have been checked against scanned images. C19-03: scan, PDF pages 142–144

His procedure gives the reader work to do. Keep something constant, alter something else, and inspect the consequence. It is a way to make a literary explanation answerable to the wording.

The following comparisons are analytical alternatives, not Qur’anic text. The two Arabic alternatives follow the constructions considered by al-Jurjānī; the English plain statement is a teaching paraphrase.

Version Analytical wording What changes
Plain paraphrase “My hair has turned gray.” The condition is stated without the fire image.
Alternative A اشْتَعَلَ شَيْبُ الرَّأْسِ (“The gray hair of the head blazed.”) Gray hair becomes the grammatical subject.
Alternative B اشْتَعَلَ الشَّيْبُ فِي الرَّأْسِ (“Gray hair blazed in the head.”) The head is presented as the location.

The instructional advantage is also the limitation. We can see that the alternatives organize attention differently. We cannot infer that the less vivid English paraphrase represents the best humanity can compose. A demonstration designed to isolate a feature is not a literary championship.

Nor should “pervasive spread” become an anatomical measurement. The expression presents aging through an encompassing image; it does not give a percentage of white hairs. A reader might accept the larger impression while declining to infer that literally every hair has whitened. The distinction keeps literary interpretation proportionate to what language can establish.

Why the image belongs here

Consider an objection that a sympathetic reading should not brush aside: fire is energetic, whereas old age is associated with loss of energy. Might “blazing” be an extravagant or even ill-chosen image?

It would be ill-chosen if the clause required every property of fire to apply to an aging man. But a metaphor selects a relationship. Brightness, spread, and the change in appearance can matter without implying youthful vigor. Ibn ʿĀshūr develops the image through a shining appearance spreading across a dark surface. He also reads the physical descriptions as an appeal for mercy rather than information God needs to learn. C19-05: commentary on 19:4–6

That last observation helps recover the sentence’s purpose. Zakariyyā is addressing the one to whom his condition is already known. The language presents his need within a relationship. One need not share the prayer’s theology to recognize this as its communicative situation.

On the reading offered here, the clause’s vigor makes the advance of age vivid. The loss of strength does not prevent the description from having force. Indeed, the contrast may intensify the presentation: the speaker is weakening while the visible signs of age seem active. This is an interpretive proposal. It should be tested against the surrounding passage, not presented as a hidden physical fact or a measured psychological effect.

There is also a difference between seeing and being told. “I am old” supplies a category. A description of weakness and whitened hair gives the reader particulars through which to imagine the predicament. The subsequent statement of confidence prevents the verse from ending with bodily decline. The prayer continues beyond what the body appears to permit.

This reading offers a reason to value the image besides its novelty. It contributes to the speaker’s position and the request that follows. If we removed it, the prayer would still contain aging and need, but one of its ways of making them present would disappear. That is a defensible account of contribution. It is not proof that no alternative could contribute equally well by different means.

The modern study of classical poetics can sharpen this distinction. Lara Harb’s publisher-provided summary of her chapter on naẓm describes sentence construction as capable of prompting discovery through implicit meaning and context. It situates Qur’anic and poetic beauty within a connected field of analysis. This is a useful research orientation, not an empirical finding about how every reader experiences 19:4. Only the chapter summary and bibliographic information were inspected for this draft. C19-06: Harb, chapter 5

Give the alternative explanation its strength

A skeptical reader may accept the entire interpretation and still say: this is what accomplished literature does. It makes grammar, imagery, and situation work together. Why should this example count against exceptional human authorship?

At this stage it does not decide between the explanations. A striking and well-integrated metaphor is compatible with human literary skill. It would be circular to define the effect as superhuman because it occurs in scripture and then use the effect to prove that the scripture is superhuman.

The fair response is to enlarge the investigation. Examine accomplished Arabic writing in context, including writing whose effects differ from the Qur’an’s. Give each passage an opportunity to succeed at its own purpose. A restrained account of aging may be excellent because it withholds the dramatic image this verse supplies. A poem may develop an image over many lines because its purpose differs from the compression of a prayer.

A comparison therefore needs two questions. How effectively does each work accomplish its purpose? And, where the purposes genuinely overlap, which differences in expression matter? Neither question is answered by counting metaphors or by penalizing another work for lacking the Qur’an’s exact features.

The strongest human-authorship account can accommodate exceptional achievement. It need not predict ordinary language, obvious flaws, or unevenness in every short passage. To challenge that account, later chapters must investigate sustained performance, complete compositions, historical evidence, and fair alternatives. Even then, literary conclusions and conclusions about origin require separate reasoning.

There is an equally important challenge to the favorable interpretation itself. Perhaps the sense of comprehensive grayness arises mainly from our prior knowledge that the speaker is old. Perhaps familiarity makes the original seem inevitable. Perhaps an unfamiliar reader would regard a different construction as clearer. These possibilities do not refute al-Jurjānī’s analysis in advance. They identify what an investigation would have to distinguish.

What measurement could add

The comparison can generate researchable questions without turning interpretation into a fictitious score. One proposed study would ask proficient Arabic readers to judge several carefully reviewed versions of the sentence. It would separate at least two tasks: an inference about how extensive the grayness appears, and a judgment of how well the wording serves the prayer. The first asks about communicated meaning; the second asks about literary fitness.

A simple descriptive contrast would be:

Δextent = mean(original ratings) − mean(alternative ratings)

Here, each average would summarize readers’ ratings of perceived extent under a predefined scale, provided that treating its intervals as comparable is justified. Otherwise, the analysis should report ordered-category probabilities or paired preference proportions. A positive difference would mean that these readers, under these conditions, judged the original to suggest more pervasive grayness. It would not measure the percentage of an actual head that had whitened, and it would not establish divine authorship.

No such study has been conducted for this chapter. The equation specifies a possible observation; it reports no result.

To make the study informative, the versions would need grammatical review, randomized presentation, and controls drawn from accomplished human writing. Some alternatives should be intended as improvements. Recognition and prior familiarity must be recorded, since simply hiding the source label cannot make a famous verse anonymous. Presenting the clause alone and within its prayer would help investigate the contribution of context, although the precise design must avoid teaching participants the contrast before measuring it.

Readers may disagree systematically. Specialists might distinguish a construction that other readers scarcely notice. Religious commitment might correlate with judgments, or it might not. The data should show those possibilities instead of averaging them away. Repeated judgments from one person and repeated versions of one sentence cannot be treated as independent witnesses to a universal claim.

One especially useful outcome would be a division between interpretation and preference. Readers might agree that the original presents more comprehensive grayness while differing over whether that is desirable. Such a result would strengthen a linguistic account while leaving an aesthetic dispute open. Conversely, if context eliminates the difference between constructions, that would narrow the claim we should make for the grammar alone.

The evidence we can carry forward

The example now yields something more definite than an invitation to admire Arabic. Its wording is available for inspection. The head is the grammatical subject of blazing. An established classical interpretation explains the final accusative as specifying grayness and connects the construction with pervasive spread. The original attribution to al-Jurjānī is verifiable. A reading of the whole verse relates its physical imagery to need, remembered confidence, and prayer.

These findings occupy different levels. The grammatical forms are observations. The account of their effect is an interpretation. Calling that effect well suited to the prayer is a judgment. An argument that revelation best explains the Qur’an’s achievement would have to incorporate this evidence alongside much more, including evidence that could count against it.

The affirmative case gains credibility when those levels remain visible. It can invite the reader to recognize an achievement without demanding an immediate verdict on origin. It can also learn from a reader who accepts the grammatical analysis but disputes the evaluation.

We have examined one clause within one prayer. The next step is to examine a complete composition, where individual choices must contribute to a whole. The relevant question will become harder and more useful: how do the parts work together, and what would a serious comparison have to preserve?

Source and review note

Source identifiers refer to research/sources-19-4.json. Six source records were inspected at the scopes recorded there. Only the al-Jurjānī source was checked against its printed page images; the tafsīr sources are digital transcriptions. Harb is cited only for the available publisher summary, not as a claim to have inspected the full chapter. No reader experiment, comparative ranking, or comprehensive literature review is represented as completed. The proposed interpretation and the original working translations remain open to independent Arabic, literary, and editorial review.

Time and Mutual Responsibility

Sample chapter 2. Research draft, 16 September 2026. Arabic and original English rendering require independent scholarly review before a reviewed edition.

A short text can be easy to remember and difficult to exhaust. Its few words may establish a situation, change our understanding of it, and leave us with something to do. But brevity alone proves little. A slogan can be brief. A proverb can be memorable. The question is what a composition achieves within its limits, and whether its different elements contribute to that achievement.

Surah al-ʿAṣr offers a manageable place to investigate. It comprises three verses. We can keep the entire composition in view while considering the relationships among its opening oath, its warning, and its exception. We need not begin by agreeing with the warning to understand how the language presents it.

Read the whole before explaining the parts

The following Arabic uses ordinary fully vowelled spelling, without reproducing all the specialized signs of a printed muṣḥaf. Its wording has been checked against the displayed text of Qur’an 103:1–3. ASR-001: Arabic text

وَالْعَصْرِ ۝١

إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ ۝٢

إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ ۝٣

An original, deliberately transparent rendering:

By time,

indeed, the human being is surely in loss,

except those who believe, do righteous deeds, counsel one another to truth, and counsel one another to perseverance.

“Indeed” and “surely” make two Arabic emphatic elements visible, at the cost of somewhat heavier English. “The human being” preserves the singular grammatical form while inviting a generic reading. “Time” is an interpretive choice we will examine. “Perseverance” emphasizes endurance in ṣabr, although no single English equivalent reproduces every use of that word.

This rendering gives access to the argument. It cannot reproduce the Arabic sound pattern or settle every interpretive question. Those limitations are reasons to explain the choices, rather than to ask the reader to trust an unexplained assertion that translation loses everything important.

What does the oath bring into view?

The initial wa- is the particle of an oath: “By …” It is not simply the conjunction “and.” What follows is al-ʿaṣr. The construction directs attention toward something invoked in support of the statement that follows. The Quranic Arabic Corpus identifies the opening particle as an oath and the next verse’s lām as emphatic. These are grammatical observations, not judgments of literary superiority. ASR-002: morphological annotation

The meaning of ʿaṣr is not historically uncontested. Al-Ṭabarī reports temporal interpretations including time generally and a portion of the day. His own conclusion declines to restrict the oath to one meaning within its temporal range. Al-Zamakhsharī presents afternoon prayer, the later part of the day, and time as alternatives. We should not turn that plurality into the claim that all these meanings must be simultaneously intended. ASR-003: al-Ṭabarī on 103:1, ASR-004: al-Zamakhsharī on 103:1

On the reading “time,” the opening establishes a horizon within which human gain and loss become urgent. Whatever else a person possesses, a life unfolds through time. Read this way, the oath prepares us to hear “loss” as more than a passing disappointment. It raises the question of how a life is being spent.

That connection is an interpretation, not an additional word in the verse. The text does not explicitly say that every second is capital or that time itself proves the subsequent verdict. Those are ways of developing its imagery. A reader who prefers “afternoon” might instead hear the approach of a day’s ending. That reading can support a related meditation on limits, but it begins from a different lexical choice.

The literary proposal is therefore specific: under the broad temporal reading, the oath establishes a setting that gives the next statement greater existential reach. We can evaluate that proposal without declaring the other readings impossible.

A judgment made hard to overlook

The second verse contains inna, an emphatic particle, and the emphatic la- attached to fī. Its force exceeds an unmarked statement such as “people experience losses.” Al-Rāzī explicitly draws attention to both emphatic elements and to the expression “in loss,” which he interprets as suggesting surrounding or immersion. ASR-005: al-Rāzī on 103:2

Notice the difference between an event and a condition. Someone can lose an object while remaining otherwise secure. To be “in loss” presents loss as a condition within which the person stands. The preposition fī, “in,” makes that interpretation available. It does not require us to imagine a literal container.

Ibn ʿĀshūr similarly explains this spatial expression as figurative enclosure. He also treats the loss as a bad ultimate outcome, rather than merely unsuccessful commerce. Here the commercial contrast between loss and profit supplies an accessible way to speak about a life’s outcome. ASR-006: Ibn ʿĀshūr on 103:2

The subject, al-insān, is grammatically singular. Al-Ṭabarī explains why a plural exception can follow: the preceding expression has a collective sense. Al-Rāzī records both a generic interpretation and interpretations connecting the expression with particular opponents. Ibn ʿĀshūr qualifies the generality with reference to the people addressed by the emerging Islamic proclamation. The grammar makes a generic reading possible; it does not eliminate every dispute about the historical or theological scope. ASR-003: al-Ṭabarī on 103:3, ASR-005, ASR-006

Our working reading hears a judgment upon humanity, followed by an explicitly defined exception. Its rhetorical strength comes partly from that order. Before a listener learns who escapes the judgment, the statement has placed the human predicament before them in emphatic terms. Whether an individual listener actually feels alarm is an empirical question; the grammatical emphasis is available for inspection regardless.

The exception changes the composition

The third verse begins with illā, “except.” This small word prevents the preceding warning from becoming an account of unavoidable ruin. It also means that the positive description arrives as an answer to a problem already established.

The exception contains four coordinated predicates: believing, doing righteous deeds, mutually counseling truth, and mutually counseling perseverance. They describe the same plural group. The syntax does not present four unrelated routes from which a person chooses one.

Nor does coordination prove that the four descriptions have completely separate meanings. Mutual counsel can itself be a righteous deed. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the explicit mention of counsel after good action as giving particular attention to something included within the broader category. His reading warns against reducing good action to what a person does privately. ASR-006: Ibn ʿĀshūr on 103:3

This distinction matters for the book’s argument. A mechanical analysis might count four clauses and call the result four perfectly independent conditions. Close reading asks why partially overlapping descriptions have been given separate expression. Repetition and overlap can guide attention. They need not be defects, but their function must be demonstrated.

The first two predicates join conviction with conduct. The last two make relationships among people explicit. In tawāṣaw, the action is reciprocal: people counsel or exhort one another. Al-Ṭabarī explains it in precisely that interpersonal direction, with some advising others. The grammatical form is also recorded in the corpus as form VI. The contextual reading is supported by both sources; it should not be generalized into a rule that every form VI verb always has an identical reciprocal meaning. ASR-003, ASR-002

The effect is substantial. A paraphrase describing people who merely possess truth and patience would leave this relationship unexpressed. The verse describes participants in one another’s moral lives. A person can give counsel and also receive it. The wording makes mutual counsel explicit; it does not specify equal authority, equal participation, or an identical role for every member.

The two objects of counsel also need context. “Truth” should not quietly become whatever each participant happens to believe. Al-Ṭabarī connects it with God’s book and obedience to its teaching. Al-Zamakhsharī gives a broad religious interpretation encompassing monotheism, obedience, and adherence to revelation. These commentaries establish how their authors understood the verse; they do not independently prove the truth of the theology. ASR-003, ASR-004: al-Zamakhsharī on 103:3

Perseverance gives the final clause a different practical emphasis. Recognizing an obligation and sustaining it under difficulty are distinguishable tasks. In this reading, the ending supplies the endurance needed to continue the preceding commitments. The sequence moves from a warning about loss toward a form of shared life capable of persisting through time. That last connection is the present chapter’s interpretation of the whole, not a separate lexical definition.

Hear the arrangement, then test the explanation

At the customary verse-end stops, the endings ʿaṣr, khusr, and ṣabr share a final r. Their preceding sounds differ. Calling them three identical rhymes would conceal those differences. The repeated wa-tawāṣaw bi- in the last verse creates a more extensive parallel sequence. The two objects occupy corresponding positions in that sequence.

These observations let us ask a better question than “Does it sound beautiful?” Does the recurrence help a listener recognize the two acts of mutual counsel as related while keeping their objects distinct? That is a plausible functional explanation. Establishing an actual memory or comprehension advantage would require a study. No such result is reported here.

The whole composition can now be represented without numerical decoration:

Movement Textual basis Proposed contribution
Oath wa-l-ʿaṣr Establishes the temporal horizon under the reading used here.
Verdict Emphatic statement of being in loss Places the predicament before the listener.
Exception illā and the coordinated descriptions Identifies the community exempted from the verdict.
Closing parallel Repeated reciprocal verb and preposition Gives truth and perseverance distinct, corresponding attention.

The final column is interpretation. A diagram can make an argument easier to inspect, but cannot turn that interpretation into a measured fact.

Consider three original teaching paraphrases, not Qur’anic text and not translations:

Paraphrase Question it exposes
“People suffer losses, but good people do better.” What happens when emphatic judgment becomes a loose observation and the exception becomes vague?
“By time: humanity is in loss, except those who believe and do good.” What is left implicit when the mutual responsibilities are omitted?
“Those who believe, do good, and counsel one another to truth and perseverance escape loss. Others do not.” What changes when the positive group appears before the general verdict?

The first is deliberately thin. Defeating it establishes no superiority over accomplished human writing. The second exposes information that can be concealed by a compressed summary. The third retains much of the conceptual content but changes the order in which it arrives. A reader might reasonably find its directness useful for some purposes.

These alternatives help isolate choices. They do not prove that every conceivable alternative must be worse. A successful comparison must allow different wording and different techniques to accomplish comparable purposes.

What a fair comparison would require

A serious critic can accept this analysis and reply: human authors also use oaths, exceptions, emphasis, parallelism, and memorable endings. The observation is correct. Counting those devices cannot establish inimitability. The relevant question concerns their contribution within this composition, and then the strength of that contribution against carefully selected alternatives.

Another critic might find the passage’s abstract terms insufficiently specified. What beliefs? Which good deeds? Whose understanding of truth? The surrounding Qur’an and its interpretive traditions supply much of that context. The short surah can summarize a moral and theological orientation without being a self-contained explanation of every term. Its economy partly depends on that relationship. A comparison should give competing texts fair access to their own relevant contexts.

A third critic might accept its force while attributing that force to exceptional human authorship. Nothing established so far excludes that possibility. Religious familiarity may also affect a reader’s response. Repeated devotional exposure could help explain ease of recall or perceived solemnity. Those possibilities call for comparison and controls, not dismissal.

Before commissioning an evaluation, we would specify purposes broad enough to permit genuine alternatives: communicate a consequential judgment about human life, distinguish a response to it, and connect individual conduct with relationships among people. Then we would ask qualified readers to assess clarity, economy, coherence, and the contribution of sound, with reasons attached to each judgment. They must be allowed to reject the proposed criteria or explain why a comparator accomplishes something equally valuable differently.

Recognition cannot reliably be removed from a famous passage. Reviewers should therefore report familiarity and relevant commitments. The study should include strong short Arabic compositions nominated by readers who disagree about the Qur’an. Raters’ explanations and disagreements matter alongside any numerical summaries. No comparative superiority is established by the present chapter because that comparison has not yet been conducted.

A reader’s experiment

Choose one of the teaching paraphrases. Write down one meaning it preserves and one relationship it changes. Then identify whether your objection concerns missing content, order of presentation, sound, or personal preference. If you think it improves something, specify the improvement.

Next, return to the Arabic and the transparent rendering. Separate three statements: “the reciprocal expression occurs twice”; “its repetition gives the two responsibilities corresponding prominence”; and “this is exceptionally accomplished writing.” The first is directly checkable. The second requires an argument about function. The third requires evaluative judgment and meaningful comparison.

The theological claim asks for a further step. This chapter contributes an inspectable example of how a small composition coordinates warning, exception, conviction, action, and mutual responsibility. If comparable achievements prove substantial and sustained across the text, they belong in a cumulative argument about its origin. Establishing that larger case requires evidence beyond these three verses.

Al-ʿAṣr leaves us with more than an isolated verbal flourish. On the reading developed here, its opening places human life within time; its middle confronts that life with loss; its ending describes people sustaining commitments with one another. The reader can now examine that relationship, challenge its interpretation, and ask what would count as a comparable achievement. That is a firmer beginning for the inimitability argument than asking admiration to perform the work of evidence.

Source and review note

The linked sources were inspected on 16 September 2026. ASR-001 is the Arabic text; ASR-002 is a modern annotation resource; ASR-003 through ASR-005 reproduce classical commentaries; ASR-006 reproduces Ibn ʿĀshūr’s modern commentary. These are six works/resources, not six independent confirmations of every interpretation. Tafsir authors share textual and interpretive traditions.

The online commentary passages have not yet been collated with identified printed editions. The sites’ displayed “601” is a Qur’an-page navigation reference, not verified commentary pagination. No hadith or report quoted within those commentaries is treated here as independently authenticated. The accompanying research/sources-asr.json records inspected passages and outstanding checks. There are no participant data, experimental outcomes, or claims of computational proof in this chapter.

RESEARCH PROGRAM

Evidence before conclusions.

Source coverage, editorial architecture, and proposed studies. Protocol drafts are not completed experiments.

Source dossier: Qur’anic language and the argument from inimitability

Research snapshot: 16 September 2026. This is the first source audit for The Qur’an Examined, not a completed literature review.

What is established at this stage

The accompanying catalog contains 65 candidate works and resources: 9 bounded passage or documentation inspections, 28 catalog confirmations, and 28 discovery leads. No complete book or article has been read in this pass. Thirty-five entries have an inspected publisher, author, institutional publication, original-text, or project record. This includes indexed records when a direct page request failed. It does not mean 35 arguments have been verified.

The BibTeX bibliography uses the same BIB-001 through BIB-065 identifiers. Unverified edition dates are omitted. Its incomplete lead entries are acquisition records, not publication-ready citations. The catalog records each item’s proposed argument role, dependence on other sources, access limitations, and actual inspection coverage.

“Passage inspected” is deliberately narrow. It includes al-Bāqillānī’s online Arabic comparison, al-Jurjānī’s scanned edition, selected tafsīr and Bassam Saeh passages, and documentation for Tanzil and OpenITI. Chapter-level verification is cross-referenced in 19:4 sources and al-ʿAṣr sources. It does not certify an entire edition. “Catalog confirmed” verifies a work’s identity from a record; an abstract is not the evidence needed to adopt its conclusions. “Discovery lead” marks a proposed reading for which no edition has been established here.

The resulting research base includes affirmative Muslim arguments, descriptive literary studies, historical alternatives, and direct criticism. An author’s inclusion does not imply endorsement of revelation. The book must earn each move from feature to function, from function to excellence, and from excellence to explanation.

ID and inspected source Immediate use Boundary on what is established

These anchors should be read in pairs: affirmative theory with criticism, proposed structure with rival structure, textual analysis with historical context. The aim is an accountable affirmative argument, not a bibliography arranged to make disagreement disappear.

Coverage and priorities

Classical inimitability and its alternatives, BIB-001–008 and BIB-026. Begin with al-Rummānī, al-Khaṭṭābī, al-Bāqillānī, and the three al-Jurjānī works. Add ʿAbd al-Jabbār and al-Murtaḍā before writing about a classical consensus. Ṣarfa belongs in the central historical account because an explanation based on divine prevention poses a different question from an explanation based on the text’s intrinsic linguistic properties. Reports about al-Naẓẓām need named reporting sources and attribution checks; no lost original is being treated as inspected evidence.

Grammar, rhetoric, and tafsīr, BIB-009–025. The acquisition list includes Sībawayh, al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayda, al-Jāḥiẓ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, al-Sakkākī, al-Qazwīnī, Ibn al-Athīr, Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ, al-Zarkashī, al-Suyūṭī, and Ibn al-Jazarī. These sources serve different purposes. A grammatical analysis, rhetorical taxonomy, transmitted report, theological defense, and reading rule are different kinds of evidence. Priority should follow chapter needs rather than author prestige.

Modern literary and structural work, BIB-027–040 and BIB-064. Read Mir alongside the Farāhī–Iṣlāḥī lineage; compare Robinson, Cuypers, Farrin, Reda, Klar, and El-Awa. Abdel Haleem supplies a contextual and translational reading program. Larkin, Harb, Vasalou, and El-Desouky supply different ways into classical theory. Do not flatten their meanings of naẓm into one modern score. For every proposed structure, preserve the segmentation, textual links, rejected alternatives, and grounds for choosing among them.

Listening, reception, and translation, BIB-041–044. Kermani, Nelson, Graham, and Sells form a separate workstream. Listener response can establish something about experience and reception; it cannot by itself distinguish textual properties from performance, familiarity, expectations, or theological commitment. Historical conversion accounts require their own source criticism. Their retelling in several modern books does not multiply the number of early witnesses.

Historical and philosophical counterchecks, BIB-045–051, BIB-062–063. Sinai, Neuwirth, Déroche, van Putten, and Nasser prevent unsupported claims about isolation, transmission, genre, or linguistic baselines. Kojonen and Anderson help separate observation from testimony and explanatory inference. Sherman is an acquisition priority for the category of imitation. These works should be represented by their strongest documented arguments, with disagreements among historical scholars retained.

Modern affirmative Arabic and Urdu work, BIB-056–061 and BIB-065. Darrāz, al-Rāfiʿī, Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, al-Farāhī, Iṣlāḥī, and Saeh are initial priorities. Saeh and selected Ibn ʿĀshūr passages have substantive inspection; the remaining works in this group are acquisition leads. This selection is a starting map, not adequate coverage of Arabic or South Asian scholarship. Persian, Turkish, Indonesian, French, and German research remain explicit search gaps.

What the evidence means for the mathematical program

The morphology paper and syntactic annotation paper are methodological sources, BIB-052–053. They describe annotations grounded in traditional Arabic grammar. Consequently, a model trained on these annotations does not constitute independent corroboration of that grammatical tradition. The 2010 syntactic-paper abstract reports a partial treebank, so current whole-Qur’an syntactic coverage cannot be inferred from whole-text morphological coverage.

Tanzil documentation, BIB-054, provides a candidate baseline; OpenITI documentation, BIB-055, provides a route to comparison texts. Neither is a ready-made literary experiment. Pin downloaded versions, document normalization and segmentation, record corrections, and audit rights. Comparable length alone does not make two texts comparable in genre, purpose, date, or transmission history.

The book should publish separate layers: source observation, linguistic annotation, interpretation, measured response, and philosophical conclusion. Confidence intervals can communicate uncertainty in a defined measurement. They cannot turn an unbounded claim about all possible human composition into a measured population parameter. A source asserting superiority supplies a claim to investigate, not a numerical observation to add to a dataset.

For structural work, register boundaries and matching rules before evaluating held-out passages. For listening work, keep text and performer effects distinct. For testimony, map source dependence explicitly. For translation, distinguish what the Arabic encodes from what an English rendering makes explicit. The bibliography therefore guides operational definitions and controls, not merely chapter footnotes.

Access gaps and the next reading batch

The main limitation is full-text coverage. Several publisher or repository pages returned access errors even when indexed metadata was available. The catalog records those failures instead of treating a listing as a reading. Al-Jurjānī’s title, imprint, and pp. 100–102 are now verified from the Shākir third-edition scan through the chapter research pass; al-Bāqillānī’s displayed pages still need bibliographic reconciliation. The other inspected classical commentaries have passage-level digital verification and remaining print-edition gaps. Kermani’s English publication date differs between the author page and library records, so the catalog leaves the year unset. Sells’s second edition is confirmed but its year is similarly unset here.

The next batch should acquire lawful full text for BIB-026, BIB-027 chapter 5, BIB-038, BIB-050, and BIB-063; collate BIB-003 against print and independently review the verified BIB-004 analysis; then prepare paired reading notes on Cuypers/Farrin/Sinai and Nelson/Graham/Sells. No purchase, expert contact, or paid database access has been initiated.

A source becomes usable for a manuscript claim only when the record includes a reliable edition, exact location, surrounding argument, a defensible paraphrase or permitted short quotation, and the claim’s limitations. Repeated claims must be traced to shared origins. Contrary findings remain in the ledger. That is the next measurable outcome: a smaller set of fully traceable claim records supporting the first chapters, followed by disciplined expansion toward the larger bibliography.

Research charter

Version 0.1 · 16 September 2026 · Working research program

Purpose

Write an affirmative, evidence-led case for the Qur’an’s inimitability that readers can examine without first accepting revelation. The project begins with the text, develops defensible comparisons, and then considers the inference to origin. The theological claim is stronger than literary distinctiveness or superiority. The books must explain that distance rather than hide it.

The agreed program comprises an accessible flagship, an academic monograph, a short illustrated edition, and a reproducible research companion. These are planned deliverables. The present package is an initial dossier, sample manuscript, and descriptive computational pilot. Human studies have not begun, experts have not been retained, and no experimental result is asserted.

Evidence levels

Level Question Appropriate evidence Does not establish by itself
Textual observation What occurs in the passage? Verified reading, morphological and syntactic analysis Literary excellence
Functional interpretation What does the choice accomplish here? Context, alternative readings, careful comparisons Universal agreement
Comparative evaluation How does this achievement compare? Strong controls, explicit criteria, competent readers Human impossibility
Historical inference What composition and transmission circumstances are supported? Dated evidence, source criticism, manuscript and historical scholarship A theological conclusion
Philosophical inference Which explanation best accounts for the combined evidence? Explicit premises and competing explanations, including exceptional human authorship A mechanically computed probability of revelation

Editorial standard

Each case study presents the Arabic, an original or attributed translation, a small number of consequential features, their function in context, plausible disagreement, and the limit of the conclusion. Arabic alternatives are always labeled as analytical examples, never scripture. A deliberately plain paraphrase teaches a distinction; it is not a strong literary opponent.

Classical authors will be allowed to disagree. Their theological schools and purposes will be identified where relevant. Modern literary scholars will not be presented as endorsing inimitability simply because they recognize literary qualities. A reported event will not become verified history merely through repetition in later books.

The reader should be able to distinguish a passage inspected in its source from a title discovered in a bibliography. A page number from a digital transcription is not a verified print-edition page. Restricted or inaccessible sources remain explicit access gaps.

Boundaries

Language leads the investigation. Composition, cognition, recitation, translation, reception, historical circumstances, and transmission supply additional lines of inquiry. Numerical patterns and scientific-miracle claims are separate research questions. They receive no evidential credit until their definitions, sampling choices, historical interpretation, and alternatives have been tested.

No findings will be described as proof that every possible human composition fails. A finite comparison has a finite scope. Conversely, uncertainty will not be used as a reason to avoid assessing the affirmative case. The final conclusion should state both what the evidence supports and which philosophical premises are required.

Roles and near-term sequence

The author is accountable for the argument and writing; Arabic specialists for independent language review; a research editor for source verification; a statistician for study design; and independent reviewers for replication and criticism. These are unfilled proposed roles, not a hired team.

  1. Finish source-level review of the two sample chapters and a short opening essay.
  2. Acquire and examine the foundational sources in the dossier, including contrary scholarship.
  3. Develop full case studies of the remaining ten editorial surahs.
  4. Assemble strong comparison texts with dated provenance and documented selection rules.
  5. Pilot rubrics with consenting qualified readers; revise ambiguous measures.
  6. Lock protocols, budgets, sample-size justifications, and data-management procedures before confirmatory recruitment.

The next internal milestone is a reviewer-ready sample package and source audit. External recruitment, payment, registration, or publication requires a separately authorized scope. Local research and drafting can continue without those actions.

Completion standard

The complete program needs verified source locations, qualified Arabic review, reproducible measurements, original studies, contrary-result reporting, historical source criticism, and independent review. Present completion is limited to the files and checks listed in the package’s status report.

Book map and edition strategy

Working titles remain provisional. All editions share evidence IDs and an underlying source ledger; shortening an argument must not strengthen its conclusion.

Target: 90,000–120,000 words. General readers, including skeptical readers, with Arabic explained in place.

The selected twelve surahs are editorial cases. They are not a random sample and cannot support a claim about typical performance without a separate sampling design.

Academic monograph

Target: 120,000–160,000 words excluding references. Expand the classical history, competing readings, philological notes, source-critical history, methods, and full results. Preserve positive and null results. Appendices contain corpus manifests, annotation manuals, hypotheses, model specifications, robustness analyses, and the final claim ledger. No final conclusion is drafted before the evidence it relies on exists.

Illustrated introduction

Target: 40,000–60,000 words. Adapt the strongest reviewed material from the flagship. Use aligned Arabic and English, word-relation diagrams, whole-surah maps, and annotated comparisons. Move technical detail to stable companion links while retaining essential qualifications in the page itself.

Novelty register

Candidate original contributions: controlled changes to expression with matched controls; joint profiles of literary objectives; phrase-to-surah functional tracing; uncertainty-aware comparison maps; and reader-accessible evidence trails. These are proposed contributions. A literature search and expert review must precede any claim to have invented a new method.

The mathematical and cognitive studies will be research articles as well as book inputs. Articles are optional publication formats, not authorized submissions.

Measuring without overstating

Protocol development document, version 0.1 · 16 September 2026. No human data have been collected. This document has not been preregistered.

A question before a measure

The research question is not whether the Qur’an receives a sufficiently high number. It is whether specified linguistic choices perform identifiable functions, whether those functions survive fair comparison, and what explanatory weight the findings deserve. Literary achievement includes relationships that cannot be reduced to frequency counts. Measurement will supplement close reading.

This document separates three stages: a completed descriptive inventory, proposed pilot studies, and later confirmatory studies. The latter cannot be specified responsibly in full until qualified specialists test whether the materials and measures are usable. The pilot-to-confirmation decisions below must be recorded before confirmatory data collection.

Domain map

Domain Observable or annotatable object Proposed question Principal confound or limit
Lexicon Word forms, roots, collocations Does a choice distinguish a relevant meaning? Root frequency is not semantic precision.
Morphology Inflection, derivation, grammatical features What does a form contribute in context? The same form can perform different functions.
Syntax Dependencies, word order, ellipsis Which relations change under reformulation? Annotation may be disputed.
Semantics Contextually licensed propositions and inferences What is communicated explicitly and implicitly? Meaning-unit coding is interpretive.
Pragmatics Address, presupposition, speech acts How does the expression act upon a discourse situation? Reconstructed context is uncertain.
Metaphor Domain mappings and grammatical realization Does grammar alter the image’s scope? A vivid image need not have one effect for every reader.
Sound Endings, phonological sequences, acoustic measures How does recurrence support recognition or structure? Orthography is not an audio signal.
Discourse Reference, transitions, repeated phrases What binds local units into a whole? Familiarity can supply coherence.
Composition Boundaries, parallel units, nested structures Does a proposed organization outperform alternatives? Flexible segmentation can manufacture patterns.
Narrative Selection, pacing, perspective, retelling What changes when a story is arranged differently? Comparators need their own context.
Translation Aligned renderings and explanations What is preserved, lost, or added? Translation quality is not Arabic quality.
Cognition Comprehension, inference, delayed recall Do specified choices affect understanding or memory? Prior exposure, literacy, and language proficiency.
Recitation Text and multiple performances Which response belongs to text versus delivery? Performance conventions are not freely interchangeable.
Ethics and address Reasons, obligations, reciprocal relations How is moral responsibility expressed? Moral truth is not decided by literary ratings.
Reception Documented responses in dated sources What did particular readers report? Selection, transmission, and institutional prestige.
Transmission Manuscripts, readings, textual witnesses Which expression existed in which witness? Surviving witnesses do not exhaust the past.
Historical setting Dated evidence for opportunities and conventions Which authorship hypotheses remain plausible? Later biography requires source criticism.
Philosophical explanation Premises and their dependence What further inference to revelation is justified? No automatic likelihood model for revelation.

Numerical and scientific-miracle claims require their own dossiers. Before evaluating a numerical coincidence, specify the unit, spelling, inclusion rules, search space, and independently justified prediction. Do not select a rule because it gives a desired number. Before evaluating a scientific interpretation, establish the linguistic and historical meaning independently of the later discovery. Neither domain contributes a result to this release.

What has actually been calculated

The descriptive pilot enumerates one pinned Tanzil representation of the Ḥafṣ reading. It counts numbered verses and whitespace-separated units containing full-sized Arabic letters. Attached clitics remain attached. Stand-alone pause signs are excluded, as are unnumbered opening basmalas stored in separate XML attributes. The numbered text at 1:1 and within 27:30 remains included.

The raw XML is unchanged and hashed. Results are numeric tables keyed to surah and verse, with an exact definition and a reproducible script. These are finite-file descriptions. No hypothesis test, human-authorship classification, semantic-density score, or probability of revelation has been computed. Tanzil representation documentation, reading provenance

The Quranic Arabic Corpus provides a basis for later morphology work. Its documentation describes annotation and verification, but the entire annotation dataset has not been imported or independently audited here. The live download page requests a contact email; this release does not submit one. Dukes and Habash, download conditions

Study A: expression, function, and controlled alternatives

Primary pilot question: can independent qualified readers reliably identify a specified semantic or discourse difference between an original passage and a competent alternative?

Begin with 19:4 and al-ʿAṣr as teaching pilots. They are familiar, deliberately selected passages. They are not independent confirmatory evidence for a general claim because the hypotheses were motivated by them.

For each item, record its communicative purpose, preserved core content, targeted linguistic change, grammatical acceptability, and unintended changes. Two independent Arabic reviewers must check each alternative; disagreements remain in the record. A variant that is ungrammatical or removes core content cannot be used as evidence that subtler arrangement is superior.

Pair the method with alterations of accomplished human writing. Include alternatives proposed as improvements and allow a comparator to use different techniques. Do not force every competitor to reproduce Qur’anic vocabulary, rhyme, theology, or structure. Choose broad communicative purposes before selecting the finalists, and apply the same evaluation to both sources.

Collect separate ratings of clarity, meaning preservation, contextual fit, economy, and sound contribution, plus written explanations. A proposed pilot instrument uses ordered responses with explicit verbal anchors, and allows “cannot judge.” Final scale and anchors will be fixed after cognitive interviews, not retrospectively optimized for favorable results.

Presentation order is randomized and balanced. Recognition, memorization, Arabic proficiency, relevant scholarly training, and voluntarily disclosed religious commitment are recorded separately. Famous passages cannot be assumed blind. Readers and passages are generally crossed; alternative versions are nested within source passages. The confirmatory model design will consider random slopes for manipulations repeated within readers or passages, subject to identifiability and prespecified diagnostics.

The primary confirmatory contrast will concern a preregistered target function rather than an overall beauty score. An ordinal mixed-effects model is a candidate analysis, with reader and passage effects and an original-versus-alternative term. A comparative claim additionally requires a prespecified contrast between alteration effects across the Qur’anic and human-composition samples. An alteration effect within the Qur’an alone does not establish a comparative advantage. Model family, estimand, exclusion rules, and handling of recognition will be finalized through pilot review and simulation before confirmation. Recognition effects are observational and will not be described as experimentally caused. Claims of equivalence require a justified margin and sufficient precision; failure to detect a difference is not evidence of equality.

Weakening outcomes: competent alternatives preserve the target function as well or improve it; effects disappear under balanced familiarity; raters cannot agree on the proposed distinction; or the same vulnerability to modification is equally present in strong human controls.

Study B: comprehension and retention

Test Arabic specialists, proficient nonspecialists, and English readers using explained translations in separate analyses. Translation responses cannot be pooled as direct measures of Arabic performance.

Use content questions whose answers can be independently justified from the materials, including plausible distractors. Score literal recall separately from inferential comprehension. Immediate and delayed retention must use a prespecified interval and attrition policy. The pilot will assess item difficulty and ceiling effects, with final questions kept out of the main comparative analysis.

For the translation cohort, randomize whether a linguistic explanation accompanies a rendering. This can estimate an explanation’s effect on comprehension. It cannot establish that the Arabic text itself has an experimentally isolated effect. Familiarity and prior belief remain recorded, and no participant is evaluated as a better or worse believer.

Sample size will be chosen through simulation using pilot estimates of variability and clustering, a prespecified smallest effect worth discussing, and a precision target. Do not select a convenient total and portray it as sufficient. If recruitment cannot meet the target, narrow the study or label its conclusions exploratory.

Study C: recitation and sound

Separate written-text judgments from recorded performance. Use licensed recordings or specifically consented recordings by multiple qualified performers. Document passage, reading, reciter, duration, amplitude processing, pauses, and familiarity. Randomize order and standardize playback conditions where feasible.

Do not manipulate sacred recitation into an artificial style and treat the resulting disadvantage as a fair literary control. Where comparable performance is not defensible, analyze performance conditions separately. Emotional response, perceived beauty, comprehension, and recall are distinct endpoints. An emotional response does not verify a grammatical claim or establish revelation.

Reciter and passage variation must enter the analysis. A single admired reciter versus a flat recording of a human text would confound the text with its performance.

Mathematical explanations for readers

Paired changes. For a defined measurement, Δ = original − alternative. Show the distribution across readers and passages, not only a grand average. If the outcome is ordinal, display category probabilities or paired preference proportions rather than assuming equal intervals between labels.

Several objectives. Let a profile contain clarity, economy, contextual fit, and sound contribution. Under specified comparable measures, a profile dominates another only when it is no worse on every included dimension and better on at least one. Display uncertainty and the effect of changing criteria. A Pareto frontier is relative to the sampled alternatives and measurements. It is not proof of unique or unreachable achievement.

Meaning per token. An exploratory ratio could divide independently coded, recoverable propositions by orthographic tokens. The numerator is not a natural constant: coders may split or merge propositions, and implication depends on context. First publish the coding manual and agreement. Never equate this ratio with the full meaning or value of a verse.

Explanatory inference. Posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by a likelihood ratio when the relevant probabilities are coherently specified. This identity cannot supply the missing likelihood of a particular divine choice. Use it to expose assumptions, not manufacture an impressive probability. Correlated evidence must not be multiplied as if independent.

Structural nulls. A shuffled text is a limited control for an explicitly defined structural feature. It is not a model of the strongest human author. Any permutation test must state which elements are exchangeable and which dependencies it preserves. If no meaningful null can be justified, use descriptive comparisons instead.

Protections against misleading inference

Before confirmation, freeze the corpus and source-selection procedure, main hypotheses, item eligibility, primary outcomes, model, exclusions, stopping rule, missing-data approach, and multiplicity correction. Use an exploratory appendix for later questions. Report all registered outcomes, including those that weaken the argument. A local draft is not a completed preregistration. Center for Open Science

For a small set of confirmatory hypotheses, choose and justify a familywise correction such as Holm before collecting outcomes. For broad discovery, report the full search and an appropriate false-discovery procedure if assumptions permit. Neither a threshold nor its failure replaces effect size, uncertainty, context, and replication. A p-value is not the probability that revelation or human authorship is true. American Statistical Association statement

Hold out complete source works or authors where appropriate, not random verses from the same work on both sides of a stylometry split. Audit topic and quotation leakage. Analyze later texts influenced by the Qur’an separately. Do not multiply the nominal sample size by treating dependent tokens or repeated judgments as independent authors.

Consent, governance, and readiness

Human studies require informed consent, a qualified study lead, an appropriate ethics determination, a data-retention policy, a recruitment scope and budget, and authorization before contacting or paying participants. Store participant identity separately from analysis data. Collection of religious commitment is optional and must be justified; report only suitably aggregated or de-identified results.

Current readiness: source and protocol development only. The present AI-assisted drafts are not independent expert review. No external registry entry, recruitment, commissioned comparison, or paid study exists. The next methodological milestone is a reviewed pilot instrument and source-matched comparator shortlist.

Interpretation

The final verse contains nine of the fourteen orthographic tokens in al-ʿAṣr under this rule. That describes space devoted to the exception. It does not by itself demonstrate semantic density or superiority. A token beginning with an attached conjunction remains one written token even though grammatical analysis may separate multiple morphemes.

The difference between all whitespace fields and lexical tokens demonstrates why a counting rule matters. Stand-alone pause or sajdah signs are not lexical words. The raw text is preserved without alteration; the filter is applied only in memory. We export numeric measurements, not a modified Qur’an.

The histogram uses a logarithmic vertical axis to keep rare long verses visible. It does not imply that short or long verses are better. There are no confidence intervals because these are enumerations of a fixed finite file, not estimates from a random sample. Representation and counting uncertainty require sensitivity analysis, not a sampling-error band.

Reproduction and scope

Run .venv/bin/python scripts/analyze_corpus.py. The script checks the SHA-256 digest, sequential surah and verse identifiers, nonempty Arabic text, and the numbered-verse total before calculating results. CSV outputs retain verse IDs and both count definitions.

Only aya text attributes are counted. Unnumbered opening basmalas stored in separate attributes are excluded. The numbered basmala at 1:1 and text within 27:30 are retained. The twelve editorial surahs do not constitute a random sample. No human judgments, comparison texts, morphology corpus, acoustic data, or alternative canonical readings have been analyzed in this pilot.

All descriptive verse-length data have now been inspected by this project. They cannot subsequently be portrayed as untouched holdout data for a length hypothesis. A later confirmatory study must disclose this prior exposure.
